paragraphs.heading: Frozen seawater
paragraphs.text: Antarctic sea ice is the sea ice that forms on the Southern Ocean. Sea ice is simply seawater that has frozen, and it is usually no more than a few meters thick. That makes it very different from an ice shelf, a floating slab formed by glaciers that can reach a kilometre in thickness. Sea ice comes in two kinds: fast ice, which is attached to land, and ice floes, which are not.

paragraphs.heading: A huge yearly swing
paragraphs.text: The ice cover changes enormously with the seasons. In the southern winter it spreads far north, until it covers an area about as big as Antarctica itself, and in summer it shrinks back almost to the coast. It peaks at about 18 million km² in September, at the end of the southern winter, and falls to about 3 million km² in February. Because so little lasts through the summer, most of it is young, first-year ice a few meters thick, though its exact thickness is not known.

paragraphs.heading: Unlike the Arctic
paragraphs.text: Snow usually covers the top of Antarctic sea ice, so it melts from below rather than from the surface the way Arctic ice does. As a result, melt ponds are rarely seen on it. Compared with Arctic sea ice, it is on average younger, thinner, warmer and saltier, and it moves around more. It has been studied less than Arctic ice, because it is harder to reach.

paragraphs.heading: Pushed by wind and water
paragraphs.text: The ocean near the Antarctic coast is usually much warmer than the air above it, so winds and currents largely decide how far the ice spreads, by pushing it north. Ice that is pushed quickly can travel a long way before it melts. Most new ice forms along the coast: as ice moves north, it leaves patches of open water called polynyas, which freeze over fast. Snowfall and flooding can then make the ice much thicker. The layers inside Antarctic ice are often quite complex.

paragraphs.heading: A trend that is hard to read
paragraphs.text: The amount of ice changes a lot from one year to the next, which makes a long-term trend hard to see, and both record highs and record lows were set between 2013 and 2023. Since satellite measurements began in November 1978, the overall trend has been roughly flat, in contrast to the clear decline in the Arctic. Within that record there are distinct phases: close to normal until August 2007, above normal from September 2007 to August 2016, and mostly below normal since then. The record summer low, 1.9 million km², was measured in February 2022.

paragraphs.heading: What drives the changes
paragraphs.text: Between 1979 and 2012 the ice area grew, and scientists link this to changes in the westerly winds of the Southern Hemisphere, which reflect both natural variability and the effects of greenhouse gases and the ozone hole. These winds drive the drift of the ice, and models suggest that changes in drift speed caused the expansion. The decline since 2016, by contrast, has come with more heat in the upper ocean, which points to the ocean playing a part. Statistical studies suggest the system's behaviour has changed in structure, a sign of what is called a regime shift.
